clue.text: Crooked pole musketeer shortened in novel

indicators.note: A shortened word has given up its final letter, so the swordsman named beside it arrives one character light.
A piece placed in a word sits between its letters rather than beside them, so what comes before this gets swallowed whole.

parts.note: a novel is a book, and this one opens up after its first two letters
Athos is one of Dumas' three musketeers, minus his last letter

explanation.walkthrough: Two words here look like anagram signals and neither is one: 'Crooked' belongs to the definition, and 'novel' means book, not new.
explanation.definitionFit: Crooked pole -> BOATHOOK: a long shaft ending in a hook for pulling a boat in, so the pole really does bend at one end.

clue.text: Lowly lord keeps Tesla in farmyard

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it inside, so the letter named next is lodged in the middle of the word before.

parts.note: a baron sits on the bottom rung of the peerage, which is what makes him lowly
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic field strength

explanation.walkthrough: Tesla is the car in the surface and the physicist in the wordplay, which is the whole trick of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: farmyard -> BARTON: a West Country word for the yard and outbuildings around a farmhouse, still alive in Devon place names.

clue.text: Just about time to support charity that's collected nothing

indicators.note: A charity that has collected something is holding it inside, so the letter named goes within the word beside it.
To support is to hold up from below, and in a down entry the piece doing that sits at the foot.

parts.note: alms are charity in the old sense: money handed to the poor
O is nothing, the zero written as a circle
T is the physicist's abbreviation for time

explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the single letter first and the word it props up second, which is a habit of down clues worth getting used to.
explanation.definitionFit: Just about -> ALMOST: 'just about' in the sense of very nearly there, not the sense of merely concerning something.

clue.text: Crew eat as if it's a picnic

parts.note: hands are a ship's crew, as in all hands on deck
to down food or a drink is to get it inside you fast

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a ship's crew making light work of a meal. The answer is the phrase for winning without effort, which is a different sort of easy.
explanation.definitionFit: as if it's a picnic -> HANDS-DOWN: a picnic is the idiom for something requiring no effort, and to win hands down is to win without breaking sweat.

clue.text: Human pope struggling with sin, trying to be better

indicators.note: Anything struggling is thrashing about, and letters that thrash about will not stay in the order they were handed to you.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, and the papal picture is only there to hold them
three more, which makes the twelve the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: A pontiff wrestling with temptation is exactly the picture 'trying to be better' wants you to read as moral improvement rather than as scoring points off a rival.
explanation.definitionFit: trying to be better -> ONE-UPMANSHIP: the art of always going one better than a rival, so 'better' here means outdoing rather than improving.

clue.text: Antelope's smell masked by even nastier one

indicators.note: One smell masked by another is buried inside it, so the letters named next sit in the middle of the word before them.

parts.note: a reek is a strong smell, and it opens up after three letters
BO is body odour, the nastier smell the clue is measuring against

explanation.walkthrough: The one you have heard of is the sportswear brand, which took its name from the animal. 'Even nastier one' is another smell, not another beast.
explanation.definitionFit: Antelope -> REEBOK: definition by example, since the reebok or rhebok is one antelope among many, a small grey South African species.

clue.text: Make happy story up with treasure at the end

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a tale is a story

indicators.note: at the end picks out the final letter of treasure

parts.note: last letter of treasure

explanation.surface: A tale with a buried hoard at its climax is sure to cheer you up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns TALE over to ELAT in this down light; 'treasure at the end' supplies the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate someone is to fill them with high spirits, so the verb means to make happy.

clue.text: Cork area, cheap house that's typical in Ireland

parts.note: a bung is the stopper you cork a barrel with
A is the standard abbreviation for area
a low price is a cheap one, and low does the job of cheap on its own

explanation.walkthrough: Cork is an Irish city and county, which is what the surface is selling; in the wordplay it is the stopper in a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: house that's typical in Ireland -> BUNGALOW: the single-storey bungalow is the default rural Irish home, so common that 'bungalow blitz' named the building boom.

clue.text: Broken ankle curtailed girl's play

indicators.note: Something broken has come apart, and pieces that have come apart can be put back in any order at all.
To curtail is to cut short, so the word beside this hands over everything but its final letter.

parts.note: five letters of fodder, taken at face value rather than as an injury
GIRL gives up its last letter, leaving three more letters to shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken ankle' is a whole picture in itself, and that is what stops you counting letters. The definition is the single word at the end, easy to walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: play -> KING LEAR: definition by example, since Shakespeare's tragedy of the mad old monarch is one play among thousands.

clue.text: Jog about with bodyguard

parts.note: RE is the standard shorthand for about, as at the head of a memo
a minder is British slang for a hired heavy who keeps you safe

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jog' is the noun, not the run: the sort you give someone's memory. Both halves of the wordplay are conventions worth keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Jog -> REMINDER: a jog to the memory is a nudge that brings something back, which is the noun sense the clue wants.

clue.text: Gun shot that ricochets to hit second target

definitions.meaning: the artillery sense, the heavy barrel on a carriage

definitions.text: shot that ricochets to hit second target
definitions.meaning: the billiards and snooker sense, where the cue ball strikes two others in turn

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one continuous description of artillery, so the seam between the two definitions falls in an awkward place: after the very first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gun -> CANNON is the heavy artillery piece; shot that ricochets to hit second target -> CANNON is the billiards stroke off two balls.

clue.text: Bananas grown at Sodom are happily taken up …

indicators.note: Bananas means out of your mind, and letters that have gone out of their minds will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder, which is exactly what the enumeration asks for

explanation.walkthrough: Fruit farming in a biblical city is a picture built purely to hold letters, and nothing in the answer has anything to do with either.
explanation.definitionFit: happily taken up -> GO DOWN A STORM: an act that goes down a storm is received with delight, so the audience takes it up gladly.

clue.text: Watering holes in prime spots along road, she sees

indicators.note: letters at prime-numbered places in the whole phrase are kept; in the first word those are places two and three

parts.note: the second and third letters of road sit at prime places 2 and 3

indicators.note: the prime spots five and seven, counting on through the phrase, land on the first and last letters of the second word

parts.note: the first and last letters of she sit at prime places 5 and 7

indicators.note: counting further along the phrase, prime place eleven lands on the last letter of the final word

parts.note: the final letter of sees sits at prime place 11

explanation.surface: A woman driving notices waterholes at choice points beside the highway.
explanation.walkthrough: Number the letters of ROAD SHE SEES from 1 to 11; 'in prime spots along' keeps positions 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, which fall as OA in road, SE at the ends of she, and the final S of sees.
explanation.definitionFit: Oases are fertile spots in a desert with water, so they are natural watering holes.

clue.text: Ring Spooner's dropping down from pine tree?

indicators.note: the opening sounds of the two words are swapped, in the manner of Reverend Spooner

parts.note: a cone is what comes from a pine tree
to fall is to drop down

explanation.surface: A cone tumbling off a pine is oddly described as a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: A pine CONE's FALL, with the opening sounds swapped 'Spooner's' way, becomes FONE CALL, said like PHONE CALL; the F sound of FALL is spelt PH in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a ring is British slang for telephoning them, so a ring is a phone call.

clue.text: Three peaks followed by a war film

indicators.note: The count says how many times the same pairing is written out before the twelve cells are full.
What follows comes afterwards, so the letter named next is written behind each peak rather than in front of it.

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop, the Dartmoor kind, with A written after it
the same pairing again, because the clue counted three of them
and a third time, which fills the grid

explanation.walkthrough: Tors are the bare granite outcrops of Dartmoor, so 'peaks' is honest. Tora was the Japanese code word radioed at Pearl Harbor, and the title repeats it.
explanation.definitionFit: war film -> TORA TORA TORA: definition by example — the 1970 epic about the attack on Pearl Harbor, told from both sides.

clue.text: Very noticeable Mark's inside with his feet up

indicators.note: The inside of a word is what survives when its outer letters are stripped off, so only the middle is wanted.

parts.note: take the M and the K off MARK and this pair is what is left
a man with his feet up is taking a rest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet up' in a down clue looks certain to be a reversal instruction. It is not: nothing here turns round, and the man is simply having a sit down.
explanation.definitionFit: Very noticeable -> ARRESTING: an arresting sight stops you in your tracks, the figurative sense of arrest that means halting attention.

clue.text: Associate of French commandos hides below

indicators.note: Something that hides another keeps it out of sight within itself, so the word named next goes inside rather than after.

parts.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service, the British army's special forces regiment
below and under are the same idea in two words

explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes 'French' look like a nationality, which is the whole point: it is a surname, and the pair were a fixture of British comedy for twenty years.
explanation.definitionFit: Associate of French -> SAUNDERS: Jennifer Saunders was Dawn French's comedy partner in the BBC sketch show French and Saunders.

clue.text: Punch weed, catching left nostril that suddenly spurts

parts.note: a blow is a punch, one landed with a fist

indicators.note: A word catching a letter has closed around it, so the single letter named goes inside rather than after.

parts.note: to weed a bed is to hoe it, and the tool gives the letters
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs from 'nostril' to the end of the clue, which is easy to miss when 'left nostril' reads as such a natural phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: nostril that suddenly spurts -> BLOWHOLE: a whale breathes through the opening on top of its head, sending up a spout as it surfaces.

clue.text: Everyone's bags in laundry switched at the start

indicators.note: in means the bags go inside the word made from laundry
switched at the start means the opening two letters of laundry change places

parts.note: to bag something, such as a fish, is to land it

explanation.surface: Everybody's luggage is mixed up in the washing pile right from the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switched at the start' turns LAUNDRY into ALUNDRY; LANDS (bags, as an angler bags or lands a catch) goes 'in' after the AL.
explanation.definitionFit: All and sundry is an idiom meaning every person without exception, so it stands for everyone.

clue.text: Fix electronic stuff that's discarded, swapping parts

indicators.note: swapping parts means the two pieces change places, the front one going to the back

parts.note: E is the standard prefix abbreviation for electronic, as in email
scrap is material thrown away as waste

explanation.surface: Repairing old electronic gear that has been thrown out, swapping its components.
explanation.walkthrough: E and SCRAP make e-scrap, discarded electronics; 'swapping parts' puts the E after SCRAP. 'Fix' is the noun: a tight spot.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrape is an awkward predicament, as in getting into a scrape, which is a fix in the informal sense.

clue.text: Small screen parts taken up by EastEnders' Lexi Pearce

indicators.note: In a down entry, up means read from the bottom square towards the top, and letters taken by neighbouring words are carried along inside them.

parts.note: six consecutive letters run from the end of the soap's name into the character's, and the entry reads them from the bottom up

explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is the BBC's long-running London soap, so the italics are a title and not an instruction. 'Small screen' is doing two jobs: telly, and a display.
explanation.definitionFit: Small screen parts -> PIXELS: a screen image is built from thousands of tiny coloured dots, and 'small screen' is also the nickname for television.

clue.text: Today trucks not starting? That's OK

parts.note: now means today, at present

indicators.note: the trucks word loses its starting letter

parts.note: lorries are British trucks

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off the news that the trucks won't start today.
explanation.walkthrough: A lorry is the British word for a truck; 'not starting' drops the L of LORRIES.
explanation.definitionFit: No worries is an informal reassurance, like saying it's fine or never mind.

clue.text: King and I upset, queen understood

parts.note: R, for Rex, is the abbreviation for a king

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: ego is Latin for I, the self
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for a queen

explanation.surface: A reference to the musical The King and I, with the queen upset but getting the message.
explanation.walkthrough: EGO is Latin for I; 'upset' turns it into OGE between R (king, rex) and R (queen, regina).
explanation.definitionFit: Roger is the radio operator's word for message received, so it signals that something is understood.

clue.text: Winter Olympics venue incredibly cold with hail

parts.note: so is the plain intensifier: incredibly cold is so cold
C is the abbreviation for cold, the letter on a tap
to hail someone is to greet them, and hi is the shortest greeting there is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredibly' looks like an anagram signal and is only an intensifier, and 'hail' looks like weather to match 'cold' but is a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Winter Olympics venue -> SOCHI: the Russian Black Sea resort that hosted the 2014 Games, a subtropical town that had to store snow in advance.

clue.text: Canteen ought to accommodate as many as required

indicators.note: To accommodate is to make room for something within, so the letters wanted are lodged inside the words before it.

parts.note: the six letters run straight on out of one word and into the next, across the gap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canteen ought' is a deliberately awkward pairing, and awkwardness is the tell: those two words are next to each other only to carry letters.
explanation.definitionFit: as many as required -> ENOUGH: precisely the quantity that meets the need, no more and no less, which is what the phrase spells out.

clue.text: Party at home hosted by friend's boss

parts.note: a do is a party, the British word for a bash

indicators.note: A host takes a guest into their home, so the piece named before this ends up inside the word after it.

parts.note: a mate is a friend, and it opens after its first letter
someone at home is in, which is the standard crossword pairing

explanation.walkthrough: Three everyday British conventions in one clue: a do for a party, a mate for a friend, in for at home. All three come up again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: boss -> DOMINATE: to boss people is to order them about and control them, which is dominating them in plainer speech.

clue.text: Chain I blunder into when reversing

indicators.note: into means the pieces go inside the turned-round word for when
reversing means the word for when is turned to read backwards

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
to err is to make a mistake, to blunder

explanation.surface: A man blunders into a chain while driving backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: AS (when) is read in reverse to give SA, and I plus ERR (blunder) goes 'into' it. A sierra is a jagged mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: A sierra is a long range of mountains with a jagged crest, so a mountain chain.

clue.text: Dragon losing a head, showing complacency?

parts.note: Smaug is the dragon of The Hobbit, and the A he loses leaves four letters
a ness is a headland: Dungeness and Sheerness are both named for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing a head' reads as a beheading, and it is not one. The dragon loses the letter A, and 'head' is a separate word doing separate work.
explanation.definitionFit: complacency -> SMUGNESS: both name the self-satisfied contentment of someone who thinks nothing more needs doing.
